No `package.json` — just 5 plain Node files, no dependencies, no framework. Here's how the pieces connect.

## The shape

```
server.js  →  auth.js  →  routes.js  →  cache.js  →  store.js
```

Request comes in, gets authenticated, gets routed, maybe hits cache, maybe hits store. Five files, five jobs.

## Each piece

**`server.js`** — raw Node `http` server. Every request goes through `verifyToken` first; no token, no user → 401 before routing even happens. Entry point is `createServer().listen(...)`, port from `PORT` env var (default 8080).

**`auth.js`** — bearer tokens shaped like `<userId>.<hexSignature>`, HMAC-SHA256 signed with `AUTH_SECRET` (defaults to `'dev-secret'` if unset — worth checking prod has this set). Uses `timingSafeEqual` for the signature check, so it's not naively vulnerable to timing attacks.

**`routes.js`** — a flat lookup table (`"GET /orders"` → handler function), no framework. GET routes go through the cache; the one POST route writes straight to the store.

**`cache.js`** — a 256-entry LRU, no TTL of its own. Sits in front of reads only.

**`store.js`** — in-memory `Map` standing in for a real DB. Every record has its own 15-minute TTL from last write.

## The thing to know before you touch this

`routes.js` line 5-6 comments say writes "invalidate the affected keys" — but `putOrder` in `store.js` never touches the cache. So after a POST to `/orders`, a cached `GET /orders` for that user can keep serving stale data until either the cache entry gets LRU-evicted or you restart the process. That comment is describing intended behavior that isn't implemented.
